governanceNotes: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY with NOT_ESTABLISHED consensus and hypothesizedOnly mechanism: the largest datasets (Mulloy claims n=11,602; Shirai nationwide n=5,331) document mood/anxiety associations with DE but are cross-sectional or data-mining designs with unknown directionality, and the psychotropic confound (OR 2.41) operates on both sides of the edge.

Pharmacological displacement guard: in any veteran presentation, SSRI/SNRI/antipsychotic therapy is at least as plausible an explanation for DE as a primary mood disorder developing after DE; the edge cannot rank these.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The claims-data-mining cohort (n=11,602) found anxiety, antidepressant use, and psychoses positively associated with DE versus other male sexual disorders (Mulloy 2023); the nationwide survey (n=5,331) found low partnership satisfaction (OR 2.27) and ED (OR 2.04) associated with DE, with psychotropic use the strongest associate (OR 2.41) (Shirai 2025); the clinical review frames DE as a disorder causing significant sexual dissatisfaction and personal distress (Jenkins 2015).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the associations are cross-sectional or data-mining products with unknown directionality; the reverse direction is pharmacologically dominant (depression itself, and SSRIs/SNRIs/antipsychotics used to treat it, are established causes of delayed ejaculation); partnership dissatisfaction is bidirectional; and no cohort measures incident depressive disorder after DE onset. Attribution requires excluding medication-induced DE before any distress pathway is credited.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized sexual-distress pathway: persistent ejaculatory delay produces sexual dissatisfaction, partner-strain, and avoidance of intimacy; sustained sexual-distress burden presents as or compounds a depressive disorder. The same dataset that supports the association also shows psychotropics associated with DE at the highest OR, meaning a large share of DE-with-depression presentations reflect treatment effects rather than a distress cascade.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Cross-sectional designs with unknown directionality; a documented pharmacological reverse direction that operates through the very drugs used to treat the outcome; partnership-satisfaction bidirectionality; and no incident-cohort data - association strength is the supportable ceiling.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Depressive-disorder diagnosis with onset chronology relative to DE; full psychotropic medication history with temporal displacement analysis to exclude medication-induced DE; sexual-distress documentation
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Medication-induced DE from antidepressants/antipsychotics (dominant reverse direction)

sourceReferences.citation: Mulloy E, Zhang A, Balladelli F, Del Giudice F, Glover F, Eisenberg ML. Diagnoses and medications associated with delayed ejaculation. Sex Med. 2023;11(4):qfad040. PMID 37547871.
sourceReferences.note: Insurance-claims data-mining cohort (n=11,602 men with DE matched to ED/PD controls): anxiety, antidepressant use, psychoses, male infertility, and testicular dysfunction showed positive associations with DE; directionality is unknown by design.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 37547871; anxiety and antidepressant associations with DE

sourceReferences.citation: Shirai M, Tsujimura A, Fukuhara S, et al. Prevalence and associated factors of delayed ejaculation: insights from a nationwide internet-based, cross-sectional survey on male sexual dysfunction in Japan. Sex Med. 2025;13(4):qfaf072. PMID 40937118.
sourceReferences.note: Nationwide cross-sectional survey (n=5,331 sexually active men): DE prevalence 5.16%; erectile dysfunction (OR 2.04), psychotropic drug use (OR 2.41), neurological diseases (OR 2.02), and low partnership satisfaction (OR 2.27) associated with DE; psychotropics are a major confound because they treat mood disorders and also delay ejaculation.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 40937118; multivariate ORs including psychotropic confound

sourceReferences.citation: Jenkins LC, Mulhall JP. Delayed orgasm and anorgasmia. Fertil Steril. 2015 Nov;104(5):1082-8. PMID 26439762.
sourceReferences.note: Review: delayed orgasm/anorgasmia causes significant sexual dissatisfaction and personal distress; etiologies include medications, endocrinopathies, sensation loss, and psychological factors - framing the distress pathway without asserting causation to mood disorders.
